title: Odin, der Göttervater (Odin, the Father of the Gods)
subject: Odin as Allfather with ravens and wolves
description: 19th-century romantic depiction of Odin as the Allfather, showing his attributes: the wide-brimmed hat, the Gungnir spear, and the two ravens (Huginn and Muninn). Romantic-era images like this one shaped the popular image of Norse gods for the next two centuries.
alt: Odin as Allfather with ravens and wolves — Odin, der Göttervater (Odin, the Father of the Gods)

title: Odin on Sleipnir (17th-c. Icelandic manuscript)
museum: National Library of Iceland (Háskólabibliótekin), MS Neustadt 97
subject: Odin riding the eight-legged horse Sleipnir
description: A medieval Icelandic manuscript illumination showing Odin on the eight-legged Sleipnir. This is among the oldest surviving pictorial depictions of a Norse god — a 17th-century copy of an older tradition.
alt: Odin riding the eight-legged horse Sleipnir — Odin on Sleipnir (17th-c. Icelandic manuscript)

title: The Oseberg Ship
subject: Viking-age royal ship burial (archaeological)
description: The Oseberg ship, buried c. 820 CE, is one of the best-preserved Viking ships ever found. Its burial goods included a tapestry often interpreted as a goddess (Freyja or Frigg) and elaborate carved panels with interlace — direct archaeological evidence of the Norse world the myths describe.
alt: Viking-age royal ship burial (archaeological) — The Oseberg Ship

title: Thor's Battle Against the Jötnar
subject: Thor fighting the giants
description: A monumental 19th-century Swedish painting of Thor in combat with the giants (jötnar), his hammer Mjölnir raised. Romantic-era painters like Winge were the first to create a 'high art' visual tradition for Norse myth.
alt: Thor fighting the giants — Thor's Battle Against the Jötnar

title: Thor and Hrungnir
subject: Thor striking the giant Hrungnir with Mjölnir
description: Thor in the act of shattering the iron-headed giant Hrungnir with his hammer — one of Thor's signature exploits in the Prose Edda.
alt: Thor striking the giant Hrungnir with Mjölnir — Thor and Hrungnir

title: Thor (Valhalla)
subject: Thor, god of thunder
description: Thor as the god of thunder, in the style of the German romantic mythological illustration tradition (Doepler, Gehrts), which dominated the visual image of Norse gods in the early 20th century.
alt: Thor, god of thunder — Thor (Valhalla)

title: The Death of Balder (Balders Død)
subject: Baldr's death
description: An 18th-century Danish painting of the death of Baldr — the great tragedy of Norse myth in which the mistletoe dart kills the brightest of the gods. One of the earliest 'high art' treatments of a Norse subject.
alt: Baldr's death — The Death of Balder (Balders Død)

title: Loki leaves the hall and threatens the Æsir with fire
subject: Loki, the trickster
description: Loki in the moment of his great transgression — turning against the gods. Frølich's illustrations were part of the Nordic romantic revival that gave Norse myth its modern visual identity.
alt: Loki, the trickster — Loki leaves the hall and threatens the Æsir with fire

title: The Gokstad Ship
subject: Viking-age ship burial (archaeological)
description: The Gokstad ship, buried c. 890 CE, a Viking royal warship. Together with the Oseberg and Tune ships, it forms the core archaeological evidence for the Norse world — the very vessels the myths describe (cf. Skíðblaðnir, the ship that folds up).
alt: Viking-age ship burial (archaeological) — The Gokstad Ship

title: Freyja and the Necklace (Brísingamen)
subject: Freyja with the necklace Brísingamen
description: Freyja with her great necklace Brísingamen — the gemmed necklace that the dwarves made and which Loki stole from her. A late-19th-century romantic depiction of the Vanir goddess of love, war, and seiðr.

title: Hel
subject: Hel, ruler of the realm of the dead
